extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (aspiring and experienced), especially speculative-fiction authors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and evaluating allegories in fiction: what an allegory is, when and why to use it, how to choose symbols, how subtle to be, and how to avoid accidental or didactic allegory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of allegory / purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that convey a message through fiction — especially where the reader might not accept the message directly but will accept the allegorical version; parables and fables (e.g., Animal Farm, Aesop’s Fables, 1984).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegories are stories 'trying to teach something' and typically use intentional symbols or stand-ins to represent real-world people, ideas, or situations. Use examples like Nathan's ewe-lamb parable (David and Bathsheba) to see how an allegory conveys a moral indirectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial intent vs reader interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: An allegory involves inserted intentional symbols and an authorial decision to map story elements to real-world referents; but readers' interpretations matter and may differ from author intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether you, as author, are deliberately creating one-to-one symbols (true allegory) or simply communicating themes. Recognize that authors (e.g., Tolkien) may reject strict allegory while still conveying themes; be prepared for readers/professors to disagree on classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask why: mission-driven vs thematic depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself whether you want the story to be allegorical because you have a mission to change hearts and minds, or because you want your writing to have deeper purpose beyond telling a good story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your primary motive is to teach/convert, you risk creating didactic work. Be honest about your aim before designing allegorical elements; too much mission-driven intent can alienate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtlety / opacity — avoid hitting readers over the head
rubrics_metrics.description: Be as opaque as possible in how the allegory maps to its referent so readers can enjoy the story and internalize the message over time rather than feel lectured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't 'hit someone over the head' with an allegory for hundreds of pages. If telling the allegory bluntly would turn readers off, make the mapping subtler so the story works on its own and the message can sink in later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work at multiple levels — story must hold independently
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective allegory should function both as an engaging story and as a metaphorical representation; there should be more going on than just the allegory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characterization, plot, and reader engagement stand on their own (Animal Farm is enjoyable for its characters even without knowing the allegory). If there's nothing else, keep the allegory short or it will feel like a polemic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid accidental allegories / check mappings
rubrics_metrics.description: Be conscious of how invented fictional elements might map onto real-world groups or ideas and unintentionally become allegorical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflect on whether your world-building inadvertently creates stand-ins that reproduce biases. If you don't intend an allegory, 'pull that thread out and re-map it.' Study unconscious biases and revise to avoid problematic accidental allegory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbol selection and thematic alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose specific symbols intentionally and make sure each use supports the theme or referent you intend (e.g., the conch representing power in Lord of the Flies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you pick symbols, check every occurrence: does it reinforce the intended meaning? Align symbols thematically rather than using them haphazardly. Avoid one-to-one literalism unless that is your deliberate style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length considerations: short vs novel-length allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: Shorter allegories can be more obvious and blunt; extended novel-length allegories need masking and layers to avoid fatigue or didacticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your allegory is brief, being overt can work (e.g., parables). For novels or series, hide layers and let the allegory emerge subtly over time; prolonged heavy-handedness will 'give readers a headache.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise questions vs give answers (story vs polemic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story should raise questions; a polemic answers them. Allegories that resolve every question risk becoming polemical and alienating readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to invite reflection rather than force conclusions. If your allegory answers everything explicitly, it shifts from story to polemic and readers may resent being told what to think.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use perspective and empathy to persuade
rubrics_metrics.description: To invite readers to reconsider entrenched views, invest them in a likable point of view or character who experiences the situation you want them to understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the protagonist sympathetic and personally invested so readers identify with them (example: Elder Scrolls Summerset expansion uses player perspective to make the issue felt). Narratively embody the experience you want readers to empathize with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory and satire overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegory and satire both allow authors to present messages readers might otherwise reject by reframing them; they often intersect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the overlap: satire can be allegorical and allegory can be satirical. Decide whether you're aiming for critique (satire) or representational mapping (allegory), or both, and use the techniques accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate practice: retell fable as allegory (homework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise: take a famous fable and retell it as an allegory by backing off the didactic drill, emphasizing characterization and themes so it becomes more story and less simple metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical application: shift focus from explicit lesson to character-driven narrative. This trains subtlety, layering, and how to keep a story working independently of its moral.
